results.title: Pre-trend analysis: Significance and symbolism
results.content: # Significance of Pre-trend analysis. Pre-trend analysis is crucial for Staggered Difference-in-Differences estimation. It involves accounting for the pre-existing trends of key variables before the implementation of Local Climate Change Policy. This step ensures that any observed changes after policy implementation are genuinely attributable to the policy itself, rather than being a continuation of prior trends. By controlling for these pre-existing trends, researchers can improve the accuracy and reliability of their causal inferences regarding the policy's impact. Synonyms: Examination, Evaluation, Preliminary study, Preliminary review, Initial analysis, Foresight, Prediction, Forecasting, Anticipation. results.title: A new synthesis and key lessons from the recent difference-in-differences literature
results.content: They note that most of the new DiD literature can be seen as relaxing some of the assumptions of the classic two-period, large sample of independent units with parallel trends, DiD model in one of three ways: introducing multiple periods and staggered treatment timing; considering potential violations of parallel trends; and departing from the assumption of observing a sample of many independent clusters sampled from a super-population. ·       In contexts with staggered treatment timing, this can also affect the estimation of pre-trend coefficients in the typical event study plot used to illustrate no pre-trends -  so using the new methods for dealing with staggered DiD is needed for looking at pre-trends here too. That is, while the new papers clarify very well the statistical assumptions needed for estimation, effective use of these methods also requires being able to understand what the threats to these assumptions are in different contexts, and to make a plausible rhetorical argument as to why we should think the assumptions hold.

results.title: GitHub - mcaceresb/stata-pretrends: Power calculations and visualization of pre-trends tests following Roth (2022). (Stata version of the R package of the same name.)
results.content: The `pretrends` package provides tools for power calculations for pre-trends tests, and visualization of possible violations of parallel trends. The basic idea is that if we are relying on a pre-trends test to verify the parallel trends assumption, we’d like that test to have *power* to detect relevant violations of parallel trends. To assess the power of a pre-trends test, we can calculate its ex ante power: how big would a violation of parallel trends need to be such that we would detect it some specified fraction (say 80%) of the time? The pretrends package provides methods for doing these calculations, as well as for visualizing potential violations of parallel trends on an event-study plot. 1. The `power` sub-command calculates the slope of a linear violation of parallel trends that a pre-trends test would detect a specified fraction of the time. 2. Alternatively, the user can specify a hypothesized violations of parallel trends—the package then creates a plot to visualize the results, and reports various statistics related to the hypothesized difference in trend. The user can specify a hypothesized linear pre-trend via the `slope()` option, or provide an arbitrary violation of parallel trends via the `delta()` option. In the command above, the option `pre(1/3)` tells the package that the pre-treatment event-study coefficients are in positions 1 through 3 in our regression results. The package’s second function enables power analyses and visualization given the results of an event-study and a user-hypothesized violation of parallel trends. Heuristically, the event-plot is more convincing if an economically plausible violation of parallel trends cannot explain the pattern in the event-study (e.g. go through all of the confidence intervals); see the HonestDiD package for a formalization of this idea. (Note when specifying `numpre()` the vector `b()` and the matrix `v()` must only contain the relevant coefficients.) The resulting plot super-imposes the conjectured linear violation of parallel trends on the event-plot in red. In either case the event study data is saved in `r()`, along several useful statistics about the power of the pre-test against the hypothesized trend. Last, although our example has focused on a linear violation of parallel trends, the package allows the user to input an arbitrary non-linear hypothesized trend.
